NAVY, TEAL, AMBER, GRAY = "#1F3A5F", "#2A9D8F", "#E9A23B", "#C9CED6"

## Four verbs turn a table into an answer

| Verb | Question it answers | pandas tool |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Select** | Which columns do I need? | `.loc[:, cols]` |
| **Filter** | Which rows do I want? | `.loc[condition]` |
| **Create** | What can I compute from what I have? | `df["new"] = ...` |
| **Group** | What does each category look like? | `.groupby().mean()` |

Our question: **which college majors pay the most?**
It is answered with these four verbs and no loops.

::: notes
Tabular data is everywhere: spreadsheets, CSVs, records. Plain lists
and loops can hold it, but every question needs hand-written code.
pandas gives a DataFrame with labeled columns, so the same few verbs
work on any dataset. Guiding question: how do a few operations take us
from a raw table to an answered question?
:::

## Our data: earnings for 173 college majors

```{python}
import pandas as pd

grads = pd.read_csv("data/recent-grads.csv")
grads[["Major", "Major_category", "Median"]].head(2)
```

**Source:** @casselman2014major, with data from the American
Community Survey 2010 to 2012 [@fivethirtyeight2014data]. `Median` is
annual earnings in USD.

::: notes
One row per college major, for recent graduates: number of graduates,
share who are women, median earnings, unemployment rate, and how many
hold jobs that need a college degree. One row has missing counts (Food
Science). Full citation is on the Sources slide.
:::

## A DataFrame is a table, a Series is one column

```{python}
#| echo: false
from IPython.display import Markdown
Markdown("""
| Concept | What it is | Example |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **DataFrame** | 2D table, named columns | `grads` |
| **Series** | One labeled column | `grads["Median"]` |
""")
```

```{python}
print(type(grads).__name__, grads.shape)
print(type(grads["Median"]).__name__, grads["Median"].shape)
```

- Rows are observations, columns are variables
- 173 majors (rows) by 21 variables (columns)
- Background: [ids-book Chapter 4](
  https://statds.github.io/ids-book/04-python.html);
  the pandas design is described in @mckinney2010data

::: notes
A DataFrame is two-dimensional. Each column has a name and a dtype. A
single column pulled out is a Series. This deck is about manipulation,
not import, so the import is one line.
:::

## Select: pick only the columns you need

```{python}
grads.loc[:, ["Major", "Median", "Unemployment_rate"]].head(3)
```

**Notice:** three of 21 columns. `:` means "every row".

- Double brackets `[[...]]` return a DataFrame, single brackets a Series
- Choosing columns first keeps later steps small and readable

::: notes
`.loc[rows, columns]` selects by label. Narrow output keeps attention on
what the question needs.
:::

## Filter: keep only the rows you want

```{python}
is_eng = grads["Major_category"] == "Engineering"
engineering = grads.loc[is_eng]
len(engineering)
```

**Notice:** the condition gives True or False per row. Only True rows stay.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 2.7
#| fig-alt: "Histogram of median earnings by major, Engineering highlighted"
is_eng = grads["Major_category"] == "Engineering"
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
bins = range(20000, 120000, 5000)
ax.hist(grads.loc[~is_eng, "Median"], bins=bins, color=GRAY,
        label="Other majors")
ax.hist(grads.loc[is_eng, "Median"], bins=bins, color=TEAL,
        label="Engineering (rows kept)")
ax.set_title("The filter keeps the teal rows")
ax.set_xlabel("Median earnings (USD)")
ax.set_ylabel("Number of majors")
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(lambda x, _: f"${x/1000:.0f}k")
ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=12)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: notes
The Boolean Series goes into `.loc[]`. It is the pandas version of a
WHERE clause in SQL. Both the comparison and the selection are
vectorized, so no loop is written. 29 of the 173 majors are engineering.
:::

## Create: a new column from existing ones

```{python}
grads = grads.copy()
grads["degree_job_share"] = grads["College_jobs"] / (
    grads["College_jobs"] + grads["Non_college_jobs"]
)
grads[["Major", "degree_job_share"]].round(2).head(2)
```

**Notice:** the share of grads in jobs that need a degree, computed for
every major at once.

::: notes
`.copy()` before assigning avoids a SettingWithCopyWarning when the table
might be a view of another DataFrame. Counts are turned into a share so
big and small majors can be compared.
:::

## Group: Engineering pays the most

```{python}
by_category = (
    grads.groupby("Major_category")["Median"]
    .mean().round(0)
    .sort_values(ascending=False)
)
```

**Notice:** split by category, average each piece, combine into one result.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.0
#| fig-alt: "Bar chart of average median earnings by major category"
rev = by_category.head(8).sort_values()
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
bars = ax.barh(rev.index, rev.values,
               color=[TEAL if c == "Engineering" else GRAY
                      for c in rev.index])
ax.bar_label(bars, labels=[f"${v/1000:.0f}k" for v in rev.values],
             padding=3, fontsize=12)
ax.set_title("Top 8 categories by average median pay")
ax.set_xlabel("Average of major medians (USD)")
ax.set_ylabel("Major category")
ax.tick_params(axis="y", labelsize=11)
ax.set_xlim(0, rev.max() * 1.15)
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(lambda x, _: f"${x/1000:.0f}k")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: notes
This is split-apply-combine. `.groupby("Major_category")` splits,
`["Median"].mean()` applies one summary per group, and the result comes
back as a Series indexed by category. Engineering is about $57k, Business
about $44k, Computers and Mathematics about $43k, and Psychology and
Social Work lowest at about $30k.
:::

## Check how many rows each average used

```{python}
(grads.groupby("Major_category")["Median"]
 .agg(majors="size", average="mean").round(0)
 .sort_values("majors").head(3))
```

**Notice:** Interdisciplinary is one major, so its average is just that
major's median.

::: notes
`size` counts the majors in each category. Small groups make shaky
averages. Also, each major counts equally here, whether it has 400 or
400,000 graduates, because we averaged the major medians. One row (Food
Science) is also missing its graduate counts, which `mean()` of Median is
not affected by but would matter for a weighted average.
:::

## What the result does and does not say

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Supports**

- Engineering leads: $57k on average, versus $40k for all majors
- Range: Petroleum Engineering $110k, Library Science $22k
- Pay and unemployment are weakly related (correlation -0.11)
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Does not show**

- That the major causes the pay: who picks a major also matters
- Pay today: data are from 2010 to 2012
- Pay for one person: these are medians per major
- Weighted results: each major counts equally, large or small
:::
:::

**Best claim:** engineering majors earn the most here. A pattern, not a cause.

::: notes
This describes recent graduates in 2010 to 2012 survey data. A group
average says nothing about why categories differ; who chooses a major,
the local job market, and later career changes would need more data and a
different analysis. The $40k figure is the mean of the 173 major medians
(40,151). The correlation between median earnings and unemployment rate
across majors is -0.11, which is weak. To go further: weight by Total
graduates, check Sample_size, and use newer ACS data.
:::

## Four mistakes to avoid

| Mistake | Fix |
|:--|:--|
| Chained indexing: `df[df.x > 0]["y"] = 1` | Use `.loc[]` once |
| Assigning after filtering, no `.copy()` | Call `.copy()` first |
| `"Engineering"` vs `"engineering "` | Clean text before comparing |
| `groupby` drops missing keys | Pass `dropna=False` |

Fastest habit: print `.shape` and `.head()` after every step.

::: notes
Chained indexing can silently fail to modify the original table. String
comparison with == does not fix capitalization or stray whitespace.
:::

## When pandas is the wrong tool

| If your data... | Consider |
|:--|:--|
| Does not fit in memory | A database or chunked tool |
| Is pure numeric arrays | NumPy |
| Needs joins across many large tables | A database (SQL) |
| Has unclear columns | Understanding it first |

pandas shines on a table that fits in memory and has clear columns.
Here: 173 rows and 21 columns.

::: notes
A correct average is still only as meaningful as the definitions and data
collection behind it.
:::

## Takeaways

1. **Four verbs** (select, filter, create, group) cover most table work
2. **Filtering and grouping** replace hand-written loops
3. **Check the output**: how many rows did each summary really use?
4. **Claim only what the data show**: a pattern is not a cause

::: notes
Return to the guiding question: engineering majors lead in these data,
and a few composable verbs showed it. Always re-read the output.
:::
